chapter.name: Agriculture
chapter.blurb: India's farming systems from subsistence to commercial and plantation agriculture; the rabi, kharif and zaid cropping seasons; the climate, soil and state-wise geography of foodgrains (rice, wheat, millets, maize, pulses), cash/plantation/horticulture crops (sugarcane, oilseeds, tea, coffee, fruits and vegetables) and non-food/fibre crops (rubber, cotton, jute); and the post-Independence technological and institutional reforms, including the Green Revolution, White Revolution and the Bhoodan-Gramdan movement, that have shaped Indian agriculture.

scope_in.item: Define and distinguish primitive subsistence, intensive subsistence, commercial and plantation farming, including the regional names for shifting cultivation
Describe India's three cropping seasons -- rabi, kharif and zaid -- their sowing/harvesting months and their main crops
Explain rice's and wheat's climate/soil requirements, growing zones and major producing states
Explain the growing conditions, uses and major producing states of the millets (jowar, bajra, ragi), maize and pulses
Describe the growing conditions and major producing states of sugarcane, oilseeds (groundnut, linseed, mustard, sesamum, castor), tea, coffee and horticulture crops (fruits and vegetables)
Describe the growing conditions and major producing states of rubber and the fibre crops -- cotton, jute, hemp and natural silk/sericulture

Explain India's post-Independence technological and institutional agricultural reforms: land reform, the Green Revolution, the White Revolution, crop insurance, cooperative credit, the Kisan Credit Card, the Personal Accident Insurance Scheme and minimum support price
Describe the Bhoodan-Gramdan movement led by Vinoba Bhave, including the Pochampally/Shri Ram Chandra Reddy episode
Read and interpret the chapter's own distribution maps of rice and wheat cultivation (major area/minor area)

scope_out.item: Impact of globalisation, WTO agreements, agricultural subsidies, contract farming or export-import debates on Indian agriculture
scope_out.reason: This rationalised, revised edition of the chapter does not carry an 'Impact of Globalisation on Agriculture' section that some older editions of this NCERT title include; none of that content appears anywhere in the extracted pages, so it is not sourced here.

scope_out.reason: This chapter's own text covers only minimum support/procurement price, as part of Technological and Institutional Reforms; a dedicated food-security discussion (buffer stock, PDS) does not appear in this chapter and would belong to Economics, which was not supplied for Class 10 (per CLAUDE.md, only the Geography component of Class 10 Social Science was provided).

scope_out.reason: These are the subject matter of this book's earlier chapters (Water Resources is chapter 3; land use and land degradation are covered in chapter 1, Resources and Development), not chapter 4; this chapter only mentions irrigation and land use in passing, as an enabling factor for specific crops.

scope_out.reason: The chapter gives only comparative rank statements (for example 'second largest producer after China') and no numeric production, yield or export figures or data tables; none should be invented.

concepts.name: Types of Farming: Subsistence, Commercial and Plantation Agriculture
concepts.description: India's farming systems range from subsistence to commercial, distinguished by the tools, labour, inputs and purpose of cultivation used.
concepts.idea: Farming in India is not one single system; it ranges from primitive, low-input subsistence farming through intensive subsistence farming to modern, input-heavy commercial and plantation farming.
concepts.rule: Primitive subsistence farming uses primitive tools and family/community labour on small patches of land, depends on monsoon and natural soil fertility, and is 'slash and burn' shifting cultivation with no fertiliser use. Intensive subsistence farming is labour-intensive farming under high population pressure, using high doses of biochemical inputs and irrigation. Commercial farming uses higher doses of modern inputs (HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, insecticides, pesticides) for higher productivity, and its degree varies by region. Plantation is a type of commercial farming in which a single crop is grown over a large area with capital-intensive inputs and migrant labour, as an interface of agriculture and industry.
concepts.example: Rice is a commercial crop in Haryana and Punjab but a subsistence crop in Odisha; shifting cultivation is called jhumming in Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Nagaland, and Bewar or Dahiya in Madhya Pradesh.

questions.a: The claim is only partly right and partly wrong. It is true that primitive subsistence farming has low land productivity because it avoids fertilisers and modern inputs, relying instead on the natural fertility restored when farmers shift to a fresh patch and let Nature replenish the old one. However, the claim that commercial farming is 'always better for the environment' does not follow from the chapter: commercial farming's higher productivity comes precisely from heavier use of chemical fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides, which the chapter does not describe as environmentally cost-free. So low productivity is not the same as poor land management, and heavier modern-input use is not automatically better for the environment -- the two systems simply trade off differently between output and reliance on Nature's own recovery process.
s: Correctly explains why primitive subsistence farming has low productivity (no fertiliser/modern inputs, relies on natural fertility restoration)
Challenges the 'always better for the environment' claim by noting commercial farming's productivity comes from heavier chemical input use

concepts.name: Cropping Seasons: Rabi, Kharif and Zaid
concepts.description: India's agricultural year is divided into three cropping seasons - rabi, kharif and zaid - each defined by its sowing and harvesting months and the crops typically grown in it.
concepts.idea: Because of the monsoon rhythm, Indian farmers grow different crops in three distinct seasons rather than one continuous growing period.
concepts.rule: Rabi crops are sown in winter (October to December) and harvested in summer (April to June); important rabi crops are wheat, barley, peas, gram and mustard. Kharif crops are sown with the onset of monsoon and harvested in September-October; important kharif crops are paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, tur, moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut and soyabean. Zaid is a short summer season between rabi and kharif, growing crops such as watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables and fodder crops.
concepts.example: In Assam, West Bengal and Odisha three crops of paddy are grown in a year, called Aus, Aman and Boro; western temperate cyclones bring winter precipitation that helps rabi crops succeed in the north and north-west.

questions.q: Explain, using the chapter's description of all three cropping seasons, how India's cropping calendar as a whole is organised across a full year.
questions.a: The agricultural year is organised around the monsoon rhythm into three seasons. Rabi crops are sown in winter (October to December) once the main monsoon has withdrawn, relying on winter precipitation, and are harvested in summer (April to June); wheat, barley, peas, gram and mustard are its main crops. Kharif crops are sown with the onset of the monsoon in the middle of the year and harvested in September-October, once the rains have done their work; paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, pulses like tur/moong/urad, cotton, jute, groundnut and soyabean are its main crops. concepts.name: Foodgrains I: Rice and Wheat
concepts.description: Rice and wheat are India's two staple foodgrain crops, each needing a distinct climate and grown in different regions - rice in the wetter east/north-east and coastal India, wheat in the cooler, drier north-west.
concepts.idea: Rice is a kharif crop of hot, humid, high-rainfall tracts, while wheat is a rabi crop of a cool growing season with a concentrated sunny ripening period; irrigation lets both spread beyond their natural rainfall zones.
concepts.rule: Rice requires high temperature (above 25 degrees C), high humidity and annual rainfall above 100 cm, and is grown in the plains of north and north-eastern India, coastal areas and deltaic regions; canal irrigation and tubewells have extended it into low-rainfall Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. Wheat requires a cool growing season and bright sunshine at ripening, with 50 to 75 cm of rainfall evenly distributed over the growing season; its two main zones are the Ganga-Satluj plains in the north-west and the black soil region of the Deccan, with major states Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and Rajasthan.
concepts.example: India is the second largest producer of rice in the world after China; the chapter's own distribution maps show rice concentrated across the eastern and coastal belt and wheat concentrated across the north-western plains and the Deccan's black soil tract.

concepts.name: Technological and Institutional Reforms
concepts.description: Since Independence, India has paired technical change (irrigation, the Green Revolution, the White Revolution) with institutional reform (land reform, cooperative credit, crop insurance, minimum support price) to modernise agriculture, though benefits have been unevenly spread.
concepts.idea: Better seeds and irrigation alone were not enough; without institutional change such as land reform and accessible credit, agricultural progress stayed concentrated in a few regions.
concepts.rule: 'Land reform' was the focus of the First Five Year Plan, with collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation and abolition of zamindari prioritised after Independence, though implementation was often lukewarm. The Green Revolution (package technology) and White Revolution/Operation Flood in the 1960s-70s raised production but concentrated development in a few areas, prompting a more comprehensive land development programme in the 1980s-90s covering both institutional and technical reform: crop insurance, Grameen banks, cooperative credit at lower interest, the Kisan Credit Card (KCC), the Personal Accident Insurance Scheme (PAIS), weather bulletins on radio/television, and government-announced minimum support, remunerative and procurement prices to check exploitation of farmers by speculators and middlemen.
